=== FILE: 'Taurine Supplements drive Cancer' - New Study, Big Claims, No Context [OIWG_OdZaD0].en.txt ===

Wouldn't it be a shame if all those health influencers that talked about Torine's health benefits suddenly had to walk those statements back? That happens sometimes, or it should happen if a person is ethical. But is that what should happen here? A big new study released just a few weeks ago indicating that torine is not only linked to cancer but accelerates cancer directly. Since torine, an amino acid produced by our body, but also discovered to offer multiple health benefits when consumed, has been making some waves for its possible longevity benefits, its cardiovascular benefits, its exercise benefits, and more. It might be surprising to suddenly see it attached to cancer. This uh study looks primarily at animal data but does also introduce human data that we'll get to. First, the researchers identified torine as being heavily implicated in multiple leukemas. These are blood cancers, especially immune cell cancers that originate in your bone marrow where your immune cells among other cells begin their life. The researchers were initially interested in the cancer micro environment, the surrounding area that the cancer rests in and around. This area is full of support cells like fibroblasts, endothelial cells, stem cells, structural proteins and much more. This micro environment releases different molecules and interacts with nearby cells to allow cancer cells to multiply and leave known as metastasis. In fact, if we look at the cycle of cancer progression and map it against these micro environment cells, we can see changes in how these support cells change over the cancer progression. On the bottom we have four defined stages of cancer and the vertical axis is the proportional amount of these support cells and the colored lines indicate the amount of each type of support cell. As one example we can see that these cancer cells known as leukemic cells progress into expansion or growth. The osteo1 lineage of cells bone cells dramatically decrease and we see more MSC's meenyal stem cells. The point here being that the tumor cancer micro environment changes to presumably support the leukemic cancer cell development. Why am I telling you all this? Well, the researchers point out that while torine is known to be produced by the liver primarily, bone marrow cells also have the ability to produce torine, implying that torine is a key molecule in cancer progression. In fact, they offer evidence by injecting genetically modified leukemic cells into mice and identifying if the mice survive longer if they're injected with leukemic cells devoid of the torine transporter or with the torine transporter. So to be clear, both groups have cancer. One cancer is missing the transporter that allows torine into the cell, effectively divorcing the regular cancer from the impact torine might have. If we look at that data, we have the survival data on the vertical axis. higher is better and the time that's elapsed on the horizontal. The blue line is the cancer with an intact torine transporter and the green line is the cancer with the torine transporter knocked out. As you can see, all the mice with the torine transporter included leukemia die. And although the other mice, well, they're not exactly celebrating their condition, they do much better with some even surviving altogether. This dams the torine transporter and by extension torine as a major determinant for leukemia's deadliness. But how does it do that? One of the primary ways that your cells end their existence when destabilizing into cancer is through a mechanism called apoptosis as well as necrosis. These are both ways for the cell to die. Unfortunately, that goes against the cancer agenda and we wouldn't have cancer if these mechanisms worked well all the time. So they clearly have been compromised. Part of those mechanisms is mediated by a family of proteins called the BCL family. They're a pretty tumultuous relationship amongst themselves. But BCL2 is an anti-apoptosis protein. It blocks cell death by binding proapoptosis proteins and sequestering them, disabling them from killing the cell. Not what you want in cancer. If we look at that data, you can focus on the right graphs. The higher the bars, the more cell death, a good thing. The plus and negative at the bottom is the presence and absence of the torine transporter. Clearly, with the torine transporter present, there's less cell death. === FILE: 1 Minute Bursts of Daily Activity Slash Your Risk of Death - Why？ [Ni6kMgMhBxU].en.txt ===

A while back, I released a breakdown of a big study looking at something called a vilpa, which is in basic terms an extremely short bout of intense physical activity, though not exercise, but through day-to-day activities like, I don't know, groceries or walking and plenty of other examples. It can literally last as little as just a few minutes. In that breakdown, we discussed how these bursts of physical activity have a noticeable impact at reducing all-c cause mortality as well as cardiovascular disease. So, I got to wondering how exactly that happens if it's such a small amount of work. That's where I stumbled across this study where people engaged in really simple exercise that simply stimulated the musculature for a few minutes at a time. Technically, they did this 20 times over, but I'm not as interested in the exercise done 20 times. I'm more interested in the first exposure lasting only a few minutes like a Vilpa. The researchers ended up measuring something called shear stress which is the friction to an area in this case the blood vessel. Think of it like a sliding force rubbing against the blood vessel wall. So what would that force be in the context of cardiovascular health? Well, your blood. It has viscosity. So it's thick and that blood rubs against the internal pipe work of your blood vessels throughout the body. But if you've been following physionic for a moment or two, you already know that your blood vessels aren't just well pipe work. Uh they're a mesh of live cells with an initial lining of cells called endothelial cells facing the bloodstream. Anyway, this shear stress is applied to those cells. So you can imagine that has some biologically relevant effect. Looking at the data, the dark dots are the physically active condition and the white dots are the non-physically active individuals. If the dot goes up, that means there's more shear stress applied to the walls of the artery. Obviously, in every exercise condition, there's a huge increase in shear stress. But like I said, what is most interesting is the initial exposure. So, the first few minutes because there's already a huge increase. Now, that doesn't sound too pleasant. A bunch of sheer stress, four to fivefold force being applied to the blood vessel wall, those poor cells. But your body ain't no wimp, and neither are those microscopic cells that make up your blood vessels. When the researchers measured what happens to those cells, they show why your cardiovascular health improves from this spike in sheer stress as opposed to beating them black and blue. The reality is, while endothelial cells, that first lining of cells, are small, they are mighty and crafty. when they get punched by the force of the blood ramming into them, they deform. And that deformation is one way they can sense to change their behavior. So to summarize real quick, short bursts of physical activity spike the force applied to the blood vessel cells like endothelial cells and changes their behavior. Okay, but exactly how and why is this not a problem? Inside your endothelial cells is an enzyme called enos. Enos is responsible for producing a potent molecule called nitric oxide. That nitric oxide when released from the endothelial cells interacts with the muscle cells in charge of squeezing or relaxing the blood vessel and convinces the muscle cells to relax the blood vessel. In so doing, blood pressure and likely shear stress is reduced. If we look at the data, if the bars go up, that means there's more of this ENOS enzyme present. And on top of that, it's been activated. And clearly we only see this increase in the physically active condition after the physical activity. If you prefer the visual image of a single cell, the top has enos fluoresing in red. Clearly there's more enos inside the cell post physical activity. So this would mean that there's a high probability that the cell is producing more nitric oxide thereby opening the blood vessel in response to the sheer stress coming from the physical activity and showing a greater ability to be dynamic. This all means this is one mechanism by which short bursts of physical activity could have an impact. Now to be fair there are some assumptions here since the type of exercise is different and the endothelial cell measurements of enos are after multiple bouts. Still clearly something is working and this is a quick mechanism that does fit. Still, that raises this question of, well, if sheer stress is so high after a short bout of physical activity and we see a beneficial molecule produced, why wouldn't something like high blood pressure, which might raise sheer stress consistently, also have a protective effect? Well, I'll bet you might be able to come up with the answer for yourself. But in the meantime, if you're interested in access to my complete analysis on Vilpa, which is vigorous intermittent lifestyle physical activity and how to use short bursts of regular daily activity, so not exercise, to your advantage in reducing mortality risk, check out the Physionic Insiders. My complete breakdown is there. Oh, and you also get access to my private podcasts, live sessions with me, weekly articles with actionable steps, protocols, and guides, and even more. Anyway, the point being it's an educational wonderland full of fairies. The link to join is in the description box. Hope to see you there. Now, in the meantime, let's get back to the problem at hand. So, there are multiple reasons for why physical activity shear stress is good and high blood pressure stress is bad. For one, I left out the word shear in the last sentence because high blood pressure doesn't always produce shear stress. It produces consistent vessel wall strain that is perpendicular to the vessel, not necessarily shear stress running along the wall. But assuming it did, there is a need to allow the cells to return to their original state. Constantly flattening the cells and expecting them to respond by widening the blood vessel is maladaptive. Physical activity sheer stress is temporary and of course leads to other positive changes. So, a simple study and certainly not all-encompassing in relation to why just a few minutes of not even exercise but physical activity can reduce our cardiovascular disease risk and by extension our mortality risk. Even short bouts can encourage increased levels of a potent enzyme called enos which associates with increased sheer stress and applied to the blood vessel wall cells. If you're interested in how to take advantage of all this for yourself, I'll link my video on a vilpas right here. So, vigorous intermittent lifestyle physical activity for you.

=== FILE: Collagen Peptides vs Gelatin [_VBWbgPmmDQ].en.txt ===

gelatin and collagen peptides though related have distinct structural differences that impact their absorption and Effectiveness gelatin is a denatured protein with unfolded linear amino acid chains whereas collagen peptides are smaller pre-cut structures of double and triple amino acids this difference means that gelatin needs to be broken down into peptides in the digestive tract before absorption possibly resulting in slightly lower bioavailability compared to collagen p peptides which are absorbed directly while both forms can be beneficial collagen peptides might have a slight Edge due to the more straightforward absorption process although admittedly there's little comparative research so this is pure mechanistic speculation not based on hard data

=== FILE: Collagen Peptides： Not Better than Protein？ [4Cvu6IRnzFw].en.txt ===

I get to ask this a lot how do collagen peptides even work how would they work differently than full protein well it's true that proteins can have all the same amino acids and even more amino acids as collagen however the unique aspect is the structure of the collagen peptide it's absorbed as a d or tripeptide and these peptides aren't simply used for protein synthesis like individual amino acids are they can bind a variety of receptors according to this review receptors like disin domain receptors integrant Lucy receptor complexes and others when it does it changes how the cell behaves increasing collagen production and reducing collagen degradation so what evidence there is does point to collagen peptides having unique effects independent of complete proteins

conditions like osteoarthritis and even general wear and tear are characterized by damage to the cartilage in the knee, the hip, and the spine. That also means that people with exceedingly low or exceedingly high LDL cholesterol may also suffer from HDL dysfunction. This is an area that's currently being investigated. I know I've been talking a while, but here's how I would approach this all based on the evidence. So, I would pay loose attention to my HDL cholesterol numbers. If they are within range, not too low, not too high. I wouldn't think about it more than that and move on to other health markers like uh I don't know fasting blood glucose, LDL, APOB and so on. If my values were very low or very high, I would not focus on trying to raise or lower them exclusively. I'd probably look at other tests like triglycerides, my fat mass, and other areas that of my health that affect my total health rather than focusing on the HDL cholesterol number itself, even if it's giving me a potential warning. The reality is your HDL cholesterol is more so a marker than something to directly target. I think calling it a good cholesterol isn't necessarily wrong considering that it doesn't directly contribute to risk, but it's more so a neutral cholesterol than anything. The arteries feeding your heart blood, thereby nutrients and oxygen and the like. Generally, the progression goes something like this. And FYI, this comes from this scientific review. Generally, your artery wall thickens as it begins filling with fats and cholesterol particles. Now, it is definitely true that the gap expands with comorbidities like diabetes, cancer, cardiovascular disease, and so on. The big aspect of the claim is not if the gap is there, though, but that it is, at least primarily, caused by sugar consumption. Now, considering the previous data that we went over, it is perfectly reasonable to blame fructose as contributing to a shortened life expectancy. However, there are many differences between Japan and the United States that could not only contribute, but be major factors. For example, Americans consume 200 to 300 more calories per day, about 50% more saturated fat on a percentage basis, and a bit less dietary fiber. So you would have this association with increased cognitive decline. The second concern that I have is that while this study is associative, they did account for many of the factors that could explain these results by adjusting for these factors. So clearly that could easily explain the more rapid cognitive decline. But the researchers controlled for that, leaving the sweetener consumption and whatever else that wasn't accounted for as a potential reason for this cognitive decline. This concern ties in nicely with the third and likely most powerful. How do these data compare in intervention studies? Essentially, if I give you a sweetener because I'm threatened by your intelligence, do we see measurable declines in your mental performance? I sure hope so. that is something that we can measure. So I did a bit of digging. So the good news is that many intervention studies on the topic indicate no negative effects even at very high doses. Yet there are still other studies that indicate worsening of cognitive performance. Unfortunately many of the studies are poor quality, failing to do the correct statistical comparisons or improper controls or giving mixed results. Understandably, this just makes things altogether that much more confusing. So, to simplify everything, here's how I would frame it. We saw that this associative study indicates a link between more non-nutritive sweetener consumption and cognitive decline, especially true for people with type 2 diabetes. We also know that there isn't enough intervention data to really make a strong case. So, put yourself in one of these three buckets. Keep in mind that these are cognition focused. === FILE: The Health Effects of Apple Cider Vinegar [1WhoBiWhdXk].en.txt ===

several years ago apple cider vinegar was hyped as a cure all by Health influencers made from fermented apple juice acvs popularity surged and fortunately researchers have looked into its health effects a metaanalysis of nine randomiz control trials assessed its impact on various clinical metrics the analysis revealed that ACV that's apple cider vinegar if you haven't put that together could reduce triglycerides by around 33 mg per desil though more specific analyses by the researchers lowered this estimate to a more reliable 20 mg per dilit while ACV showed no significant effects on LDL cholesterol it did improve blood sugar levels and long-term measures like HbA1c however effects on blood insulin and insulin resistance were inconclusive due to limited data it's noteworthy that most studies involved individuals with type 2 diabetes suggesting that while ACV can be beneficial its effects may not be as pronounced in non diabetics overall on these metrics if you like ACV it's a nice addition and if you don't you'd be better served using other interventions that likely have better evidence and stronger effects

=== FILE: Using Fungicide (Cycloheximide) to Measure Protein Degradation [fWrFMq-XU4M].en.txt ===

hi welcome to fizzy onic where we learn the body from the macro to the micro I'd like to take a moment and dive into the scientists toolkit to discuss an experiment by which scientists can measure the degradation or loss of protein within a sample if that sample is a tissue like muscle brain or something else or cells that are on a plate learn your body a science-based education in this experiment we will be using a fungicide or a fungus killer that is produced by a bacteria this fungicide is called cycloheximide but there are other compounds out there that can accomplish similar results to how we will use it for this experiment in this experiment we are trying to measure the rate of protein breakdown in a sample so as an example let's say we have cells on a plate and these cells are surrounded by media otherwise stated cells surrounded by liquid that contains the nutrients for cells to continue living we can take these cells and quantify the amount of a particular or all protein in these cells as a baseline measure of protein within the cells now we have one time point the baseline and we want to measure protein degradation or breakdown so we simply add cycloheximide to the media surrounding the cells and the cells take it up and then we wait varying times and measure protein what is cycloheximide in this case doing well cycloheximide has a chemical structure that allows it to bind ribosomes that are responsible for the synthesis of new proteins by linking together amino acid after amino acid until a protein chain is formed normally this process goes by uninterrupted until protein chains are completed and ready for processing during this process a factor known as eukaryotic elongation factor binds the ribosome and allows the use of energy to move the ribosome down I've become accustomed due to so many studies pointing in one direction to seeing the Mediterranean diet do all kinds of good for human health, but today may be an exception, at least in a relative sense. I've been doing uh more research into arthritis lately, and according to one randomized control trial, another diet, a low carbohydrate diet, may be the antidote to arthritis that the Mediterranean diet is not. We'll get into why as well as what to take away from this study because there are some intriguing reasons why. Psoriasis is the most common autoinflammatory disease in the world and it's a multiffactorial condition as with many, but it's generally characterized as an overactivation of immune cells, especially T- helpper cells and TH7 T- cells. So these are part of our more specialized adaptive immune system that invade into our skin as one site at least. Once activated, these uh cells mass-produce inflammation molecules called cytoines like interlucan 1, interlucan 6, 23 for dendritic cells, 22, 17 and other cytoines. This uh overp production of these molecules leads to hyperp proliferation and angioenesis in more understandable terms mass production of skin cells. So keratinocytes that leads to the buildup of immature skin cells creating that scaly plaque looking formation on the skin that some people experience in psoriasis. Now the relationship to arthritis is a similar infiltration that can occur in the joints leading to the activation of synenovioittes cells in the joint responsible for producing the lubricating fluid in your joints called synenovial fluid as well as collagen and different proteins that make up your joint structure. If these cells proliferate aggressively, they can form a much thicker layer in the joint that invades into the cartilage and pushes against the bones, breaking down those structures to make room in effect. So it disturbs the integrity of the joint. So the big picture is if we can reduce this uh specific inflammatory cascade surrounding these tea cells, we might be able to prevent these skin and joint issues from happening. So in this study, the researchers recruited overweight people with seroriatic arthritis in their 50s and had them follow two diets. So for eight weeks, they were instructed to consume a ketogenic or very low carbohydrate diet and then they did a wash out where they returned to their previous diet for 6 weeks and after those six weeks they were placed on a Mediterranean diet. This is called a crossover design because the same participants are exposed to both diets. We'll discuss some nuances of both diets later on as well. So, the researchers measured a bunch of inflammatory cytoines before and after each diet, as well as even more importantly, arthritis symptoms. Unsurprisingly, both diets led to significant improvements in weight, fat mass, visceral fat, improved liver enzymes, and more. But there were largely no differences between groups. These regions of your heart control your heart rhythm and the vagus nerve actually slows your heart down. So more veagal tone or input, the slower your heart rate.
